title: The Village Kitchen
hook: A young woman filmed herself growing, cooking and making things by hand in rural Sichuan. Without saying a word in English, she reached more subscribers than any Chinese-language channel.
situation: Chinese creators were rarely seen outside China, because the biggest Chinese platforms are separate from the West’s. Rural life was not seen as glamorous content.
exchange: Li Ziqi began filming in 2016, at first on her own, making slow, beautiful films about traditional food and crafts in her village with her grandmother. They had almost no dialogue, so they needed no translation.
brought: Li Ziqi
Skill, patience and films that felt like paintings, made with very little at the start.
Her audience
Viewers across the world who found calm in her work, and Chinese platforms where she was even bigger.
turning_point: In January 2021 Guinness World Records recognised her channel as having the most subscribers for a Chinese-language YouTube channel, at 14.1 million.
metric_label: YouTube subscribers, a Guinness World Record for a Chinese-language channel
measure: Subscribers recorded by Guinness World Records in January 2021
evidence: The record is documented by Guinness World Records. Her commercial business, including food products sold in China, is reported but not published in detail.
lesson: Images travel where language can’t. Content without dialogue can find a global audience from anywhere.
take: Li Ziqi is the case I’d show anyone who thinks the creator economy is American. A woman in a Sichuan village made some of the most beautiful content on the platform, and the world found her.

title: Mukbang
hook: A woman in Seoul ate dinner on a live stream every night. Viewers sent virtual gifts worth thousands of dollars a month.
situation: In South Korea many people lived and ate alone. Live streaming platforms like AfreecaTV let viewers send hosts virtual items that converted to cash.
exchange: Park Seo-yeon, broadcasting as The Diva, ate large meals live while chatting to viewers, who kept her company and she kept them company. The format was called mukbang, from the Korean for eating broadcast.
brought: The Diva
Hours of live company over a shared meal.
AfreecaTV
Virtual gifts, called star balloons, that let viewers pay the host directly.
turning_point: In 2014 international media reported she earned about $9,000 a month from viewers’ gifts. Mukbang spread worldwide onto YouTube and became one of the platform’s best-known formats.
metric_label: Reported monthly earnings from viewers’ gifts, 2014
measure: Earnings as reported in the press in 2014, not confirmed by the platform
evidence: The figure was widely reported, including by the South China Morning Post. It shows viewer-funded income on a live platform years before Western platforms adopted similar features.
lesson: Company is a service people will pay for. Formats that keep people company travel across cultures.
take: Mukbang shows that live tipping, now common everywhere, was a mature business in Korea first. The West copied the format and the payment model.

title: The First Virtual YouTuber
hook: An animated girl introduced herself as a virtual YouTuber. She started a genre with millions of fans worldwide.
situation: YouTube stars were people on camera. Japanese animation and motion capture were sophisticated, but no one had combined them into a creator persona.
exchange: In December 2016 a Japanese company launched Kizuna AI, an animated character voiced and performed live by a real person, who called herself a virtual YouTuber and made videos like any other creator.
brought: Kizuna AI’s team
A character, a voice and motion capture that let the avatar move naturally.
Her fans
An audience that embraced a creator who was a character.
turning_point: The term VTuber spread, and agencies such as Hololive built rosters of virtual creators whose live streams and fan gifts became one of YouTube’s biggest categories.
measure: A date. Revenue of the genre is reported by agencies, not for her alone
evidence: Her launch and influence are documented by Virtual Humans and others. Later disputes over the voice performer raised questions about who owns a virtual creator.
lesson: A creator can be a character, if the performance is real. Agree who owns the character before it becomes valuable.
take: VTubers are the creator economy’s most original invention outside the West. They also raise the ownership question in its sharpest form: the performer or the company?

title: Brazil’s Biggest YouTuber
hook: A young man from one of Brazil’s poorest states made comedy videos in his room. He became the most subscribed YouTuber in the country.
situation: Brazilian entertainment was dominated by television networks in Rio and São Paulo. A comedian from the north-east had little route onto national television.
exchange: Whindersson Nunes began posting comedy and music parodies about everyday life in his home region, in his own accent and humour.
brought: Whindersson Nunes
Relatable comedy and a voice from a region television ignored.
Brazilian viewers
One of YouTube’s largest national audiences, eager for creators who sounded like them.
turning_point: In 2016 his channel became the most subscribed in Brazil and one of the most subscribed in the world, leading to sold-out live tours and film roles.
metric_label: Most subscribed YouTube channel in Brazil, 2016
measure: A subscriber ranking, recorded in Tubefilter’s global charts
evidence: His ranking is recorded in Tubefilter’s monthly lists. Tour and other income is reported in the press but not published.
lesson: Regional voices find national audiences online. Brands should look for creators who speak like the people they want to reach.
take: Whindersson is what happens when the gatekeepers are bypassed. Brazil’s biggest comedian came from the place its television never looked.

title: Africa’s First Million
hook: A Nigerian filmmaker shot short sketches on a small budget with his family. His was the first African comedy channel to a million subscribers.
situation: Nigeria had a huge film industry, Nollywood, but African creators were barely visible on YouTube’s global charts, and advertising rates in Africa were low.
exchange: Mark Angel wrote and filmed short comedy sketches in Port Harcourt, often starring his young cousin Emmanuella, whose comic timing made the videos spread across Africa and beyond.
brought: Mark Angel
Writing, direction and a habit of short, punchy sketches.
His cast and audience
Performers audiences loved, and viewers across Africa and its diaspora.
turning_point: In 2017 Mark Angel Comedy became the first African comedy channel to reach a million subscribers, and later one of the most subscribed channels on the continent.
metric_label: Subscribers, the first African comedy channel to get there, 2017
measure: A subscriber milestone reported by Nigerian media
evidence: The milestone is documented by The Guardian Nigeria and Pulse. Earnings were reported only as estimates.
lesson: Short, universal comedy travels across borders. Low production costs make it possible to publish often and learn fast.
take: Mark Angel proved that an African creator could build a global audience from a phone camera and a good script. Many African creators followed.

title: Southeast Asia’s First Ten Million
hook: An Indonesian vlogger from a family of eleven siblings became the first person in Southeast Asia with ten million YouTube subscribers.
situation: Indonesia has one of the world’s largest online populations, but its creators were rarely counted among YouTube’s leaders.
exchange: Atta Halilintar posted vlogs, pranks and family content, including his large family known as Gen Halilintar, building a fanbase he called ASHIAP Nation.
brought: Atta Halilintar
Constant uploads, a named fan community and family members who were creators too.
Indonesian viewers
A vast, young and fast-growing audience on mobile.
turning_point: In February 2019 he became the first person in Southeast Asia to reach ten million subscribers, and passed twenty million within a year.
metric_label: Subscribers, the first in Southeast Asia, February 2019
measure: A subscriber milestone reported by The Jakarta Post and others
evidence: The milestone is documented. Revenue was discussed in Indonesian business media as estimates.
lesson: Large domestic markets build creators who can rival the West. Look at creators by country, not only by global ranking.
take: Atta is a reminder that the biggest creator in a market of 270 million people may be someone most Western marketers have never heard of.

title: YouTube vs TikTok
hook: An Indian YouTuber roasted a TikTok star. YouTube removed the video, and his fans took it out on TikTok’s app rating.
situation: In 2020 India’s YouTubers and TikTokers were in a public rivalry over which platform’s creators were more talented.
exchange: Ajey Nagar, known as CarryMinati, posted a roast of a TikTok creator in May 2020 that became one of the most viewed and liked videos in India within days.
brought: CarryMinati
Fast, loud roasts in Hindi, and one of India’s largest YouTube audiences.
His fans
A community that acted in his defence when the video came down.
turning_point: YouTube removed the video for breaching its harassment rules. His fans responded with a campaign of one-star reviews that pushed TikTok’s Google Play rating down sharply until Google removed millions of reviews.
metric_label: How quickly the video became one of India’s most viewed, and was removed
measure: A timeline. View and like counts were reported but the video is no longer available
evidence: The removal and the rating campaign are documented by afaqs, Business Insider India and Bloomberg. Exact figures varied between reports.
lesson: A loyal community can move a platform’s numbers in days. Work with creators who can steer their fans, not just summon them.
take: This case shows the power and the danger of a mobilised fanbase, a month before India banned TikTok altogether, in Edition 04.

title: Crisps, Sunglasses and a Phone
hook: A Kenyan student filmed herself laughing and eating crisps in sunglasses. Within months she had a deal with Rihanna’s Fenty.
situation: Global fashion brands rarely found talent in Nairobi, and comedy stardom usually needed a studio, an agent and a television slot.
exchange: Elsa Majimbo posted short, deadpan monologues filmed on her phone during lockdown in 2020, often wearing sunglasses and eating crisps, mocking everyday life and herself.
brought: Elsa Majimbo
A distinct voice and videos that cost almost nothing to make.
Global brands
Fenty, then others, who wanted her humour and her audience.
turning_point: In September 2020 she signed a deal with Fenty, followed by work with luxury brands and an E! People’s Choice Awards nomination.
measure: A date. The value of the deals was not disclosed
evidence: Her deals and nomination are documented by The Star Kenya, OkayAfrica and others. Their value is not public.
lesson: A phone and a voice are enough. Brands searching for authentic talent should look far beyond the usual cities.
take: Elsa Majimbo is the smallest budget in the archive and one of the fastest routes to global brands. She is what the creator economy promised everyone.

title: The Lipstick King
hook: A former cosmetics shop assistant sold products on a live stream. In twelve hours he sold goods worth about $1.7 billion.
situation: In the West, influencer marketing meant posts and links. In China, live shopping streams on Taobao Live had become a main way to buy, with hosts selling to millions in real time.
exchange: Li Jiaqi, known as Austin Li and the Lipstick King after testing hundreds of lipsticks on his own lips, hosted marathon live streams presenting products and negotiating prices for his viewers.
brought: Austin Li
Product knowledge, energy and a reputation for getting viewers the best price.
Taobao Live and brands
Checkout inside the stream and discounts brands offered for his audience.
turning_point: During the presale for Singles Day in October 2021 he sold about 10.6 billion yuan, around $1.7 billion, in a single twelve-hour stream, as reported.
metric_label: Goods sold in one twelve-hour stream, October 2021, as reported
measure: Gross merchandise value reported by Chinese data firms and the press. It includes presale orders, some of which may be returned
evidence: The figures were widely reported, including by Business Insider and the South China Morning Post. Gross sales, returns and the host’s share are not separated.
lesson: When buying happens inside the content, the creator becomes the shop. Western live shopping is still learning what China already knows.
take: Austin Li is the most commercially powerful single creator in this archive. He shows where creator commerce goes when the checkout sits inside the stream.

title: The Man Who Never Says a Word
hook: A factory worker who lost his job in lockdown answered overcomplicated life hacks with a shrug. He became the most followed person on TikTok.
situation: TikTok’s biggest stars were American teenagers dancing. Khaby Lame, born in Senegal and raised in Italy, had been laid off from a factory job in 2020.
exchange: He stitched videos of absurd life hacks and responded by doing the task the obvious way, without speaking, ending with an open-handed gesture that needed no translation.
brought: Khaby Lame
A deadpan expression and a format that worked in every language.
TikTok
A stitch feature that let him reply to other people’s videos.
turning_point: In June 2022 he passed Charli D’Amelio to become the most followed person on TikTok, with over 142 million followers, and went on to deals with global brands.
metric_label: Most followed account on TikTok, June 2022
measure: A follower ranking reported by Tubefilter and others
evidence: The ranking is documented. His brand deals were widely reported but their value was not disclosed.
lesson: A silent joke is a global joke. Formats that need no words travel furthest and fastest.
take: Khaby Lame closes the archive because he is everything this edition is about: no budget, no language barrier and no gatekeeper, and he still became the biggest creator on the platform.
